local.title: The Clark County jail
local.lead: Clark County is about to decide what to do about its jail. What gets built will shape daily life inside for decades.

facts.v: Built in 1985 and rated for 49 people; the state recommends no more than 35 to keep it staffed. In May 2026 there were 44 on the roster, 9 of them held in other counties.

A 2024 professional assessment found overcrowding, understaffing, and constitutional violations, including black mold in a shower; the population had been above maximum capacity for 16 straight months.
The sheriff says a new jail with at least double the capacity would be the ideal solution, with public education before any funding request. No cost or site has been announced (Docket #17).
The 2026 budget carries $676,423 for the jail in the General Fund and $663,891 in jail maintenance and construction funds — about $75 a bed a day.
Arkansas pays counties $40 a day to hold state prisoners waiting for a prison bed; the statewide backlog reached 2,299 in May 2024.
No garden, education, or job-training program inside the jail was found documented — not found yet, not absent (Docket #18).

proposals.title: Grow it, cook it, give it: a jail garden
proposals.summary: Start what Smith and Garland counties already run: an offered garden crew growing vegetables for the jail’s own kitchen and for Clark County’s food pantries, with kitchen training to go with it.
proposals.why_here: In Texas, Smith County’s jail garden gives all its produce to the East Texas Food Bank — in excess of 160,000 pounds, the food bank’s CEO estimated — and Garland County’s jail is a University of Arkansas agriculture site feeding Project Hope. Clark County has a University of Arkansas extension office in Arkadelphia with a Master Gardener program — the same kind of partner — and four food pantries already listed on this site.
proposals.first_step: Ask the sheriff and the quorum court to start a small garden on land near the jail with the Clark County Extension office, and to set aside growing space in the new jail’s site plan from day one.
limits: The current jail sits on a small in-town lot; a real garden needs nearby land or space at the new jail’s site.
It needs supervision, tools, water, and security planning — and shade, water, and rest in the heat.
Offered, never forced: the crew is a choice.

ask.label: Weigh in: should Clark County start a jail garden?

proposals.title: An offered work crew that builds homes
proposals.summary: Every morning the crew is offered: wake up, eat, and go build — or stay in the cell. Crew members earn pay and real credentials working alongside a licensed builder on homes for local families, through a partner like Habitat for Humanity or a community land trust. Some will stick with it after release; either way, the community gets stronger.
math: Labor per modest 1,200 sq ft house (trainee crew, ordinary construction)
Houses a year the crew could build
limits: Labor isn’t the limit — money is. At the national average of about $162 a square foot, a 1,200 sq ft house costs roughly $190,000 to build; materials, licensed electricians and plumbers, permits, and land still need funding.
Most people are held for weeks, so the crew is always partly new; it needs paid, trained crew leads — often people who stayed on after release.
Houses given to families work best through a nonprofit or land trust; what a county itself may give away is a question for a lawyer.
proposals.first_step: Clark County has no Habitat for Humanity affiliate we could find. A small community land trust or nonprofit could partner with the crew and a licensed builder.

proposals.title: Build the new jail as a school
proposals.summary: Design the new jail with classrooms, a trade shop, a kitchen that trains cooks, and garden space from day one — and partner with a nearby college for short credentials that continue after release.
proposals.why_here: The county is already planning a new jail. Space for learning and work costs least when it’s designed in, not retrofitted.
proposals.first_step: Ask the quorum court and sheriff to include classroom, shop, kitchen, and garden space in the new jail’s design, and invite a nearby college to plan credentials with it.

ask.label: Weigh in on the new jail

proposals.title: A door you can walk in
proposals.summary: Some people know they need structure before a crime ever happens. Offer a voluntary live-in program — housing, work, training, recovery — that a person can choose to enter and is free to leave. Choosing structure without a record is honor preserved.
limits: Nobody can be locked up without a crime or a court order, so it must stay a door that opens both ways.
“Voluntary” can be bent by desperation or a judge’s pressure; the design must guard against both.
Residents’ work must be paid and for their own growth — never unpaid labor for a company.
